headline: Police chief unplugs Flock cameras after company ignores contract cancellation
summary: Plymouth City Council voted to end its Flock contract, but the company failed to respond to demands to remove its cameras. The police chief took matters into his own hands.
details: Plymouth City Council unanimously voted to end its contract with Flock Safety in September 2026. However, the company failed to respond to the city's demands to remove its cameras, prompting direct action from the police chief.

Plymouth Police Chief Eric Fadden stated that after the city suspended Flock accounts and notified the company of the cancellation, there was no response for over a week. Consequently, he directed staff to physically disconnect the cameras' power cords to ensure they were non-functional.

This incident follows multiple controversies surrounding Flock cameras, including alleged misuse by officers and mistaken vehicle stops based on AI algorithms. Critics have raised privacy concerns and urged city councils to remove the cameras.
Dayton, another Minnesota city, has also paused its Flock program and disabled its devices after the company proceeded with camera replacements despite being instructed not to.
caption:
A police chief had to physically unplug Flock cameras after the company ignored a contract cancellation. The city council had voted to end the service.

Plymouth City Council unanimously voted to end its contract with Flock Safety in September 2026. However, the company failed to respond to the city's demands to remove its cameras, prompting direct action from the police chief.

Plymouth Police Chief Eric Fadden stated that after the city suspended Flock accounts and notified the company of the cancellation, there was no response for over a week. Consequently, he directed staff to physically disconnect the cameras' power cords to ensure they were non-functional.

This incident follows multiple controversies surrounding Flock cameras, including alleged misuse by officers and mistaken vehicle stops based on AI algorithms. Critics have raised privacy concerns and urged city councils to remove the cameras.

Dayton, another Minnesota city, has also paused its Flock program and disabled its devices after the company proceeded with camera replacements despite being instructed not to.
